item.description: Melatonin is more than a sleep aid. See what research says about its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects on CRP, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, and how to track your levels.

item.title: Is Walking Enough to Lose Weight?
item.description: Can walking alone help you lose weight? An honest look at what step counts, pace, and duration really do, plus walking's metabolic and anti-inflammatory perks.

item.title: Diverticulitis and Inflammation: When Gut Pouches Become a Problem
item.description: How diverticulosis becomes diverticulitis, the role of fiber and the gut microbiome, and how CRP tracks inflammation. Track your inflammation at home with Sensa.

item.title: How Much Protein Do You Really Need to Lose Weight?
item.description: How much protein do you need to lose weight? Research supports roughly 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg for most adults in a deficit. Learn targets, sources, and myths.

item.title: Cortisol and Belly Fat: How Stress Reshapes Your Waistline
item.description: Chronic stress keeps cortisol elevated, and visceral belly fat is especially rich in cortisol receptors. Learn how the stress hormone reshapes your waistline.

item.title: Yo-Yo Dieting: Why Weight Cycling Fuels Inflammation
item.description: Weight cycling can worsen body composition and raise inflammatory markers over time. Learn why yo-yo dieting fuels inflammation and how to exit the cycle with Sensa.

item.title: Can Inflammation Make It Harder to Lose Weight?
item.description: Chronic inflammation can blunt leptin and insulin signaling and slow fat loss. Learn how the inflammation-weight loop works and how to break it. Track CRP with Sensa.

item.title: How Are Migraines Linked to Inflammation?
item.description: Migraine involves neurogenic inflammation. During an attack, the trigeminovascular system releases CGRP and other peptides that inflame blood vessels around the brain. Here is how it works.

item.title: Is Soy Inflammatory? What the Research Actually Shows
item.description: Soy is not inflammatory for most people, and it may modestly lower inflammation. A meta-analysis of soy isoflavones found no overall rise in C-reactive protein, with reductions in older adults and those with elevated CRP. Here is the evidence, including the whole vs processed soy distinction.

item.title: Is Olive Oil Anti-Inflammatory? The Oleocanthal Evidence
item.description: Yes, extra virgin olive oil is one of the strongest evidence-backed anti-inflammatory foods. Its compound oleocanthal blocks COX enzymes like ibuprofen, and trials show regular intake lowers CRP and IL-6.

item.title: Is Honey Anti-Inflammatory? An Honest Look at the Evidence
item.description: Honey contains antioxidant phenolic compounds and shows small benefits when it replaces other sugars, but the anti-inflammatory evidence is weak and honey is still about 80 percent sugar. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is Green Tea Anti-Inflammatory? What the EGCG Evidence Really Says
item.description: Green tea contains EGCG, a catechin with clear anti-inflammatory activity in the lab. But meta-analyses of human trials found green tea did not significantly lower CRP. Here is the honest, evidence-based picture.

item.title: Is Gluten Inflammatory? What the Science Says
item.description: Gluten is inflammatory for people with celiac disease, wheat allergy, or gluten sensitivity, but for the general population current evidence does not show gluten driving inflammation. Whole grains are linked to lower CRP. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Ginger Anti-Inflammatory? What the Research on Gingerols Shows
item.description: Yes, ginger has real anti-inflammatory evidence. Its gingerols block the COX and LOX pathways, and a 12-week randomized trial found 1 gram of ginger powder daily lowered hs-CRP. Here is what the science supports.

item.title: Is Garlic Anti-Inflammatory? The Allicin and Aged Garlic Evidence
item.description: Yes, garlic is anti-inflammatory with solid trial evidence. Its organosulfur compounds, including allicin, lower CRP. A meta-analysis of 9 trials found garlic reduced C-reactive protein by about 0.8 mg/L.

item.title: Is Dairy Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: For most people dairy is not inflammatory, and fermented dairy like yogurt may lower inflammation. A 2022 review found dairy had the most favorable inflammatory profile of any animal food group. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Corn Inflammatory? Whole Corn vs Refined Corn
item.description: Whole corn is not inflammatory and is mildly anti-inflammatory, while refined corn products behave differently. Higher whole-grain intake is linked to lower C-reactive protein and higher refined-grain intake to higher CRP. Here is the whole-vs-refined breakdown.

item.title: Breathwork and Inflammation: Can Breathing Techniques Lower Your Inflammatory Load?
item.description: Slow breathing activates the vagus nerve and the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, and the Wim Hof method has shown effects on cytokines in a small trial. Here is what the evidence supports.

item.title: Can CRP Be Too Low? Why a Low Score Is Good News
item.description: A very low hs-CRP below 1 mg/L is generally a good sign of low inflammatory and cardiovascular risk. There is no established harm from a low CRP. Here is what the number really means.

item.title: CRP and Autoimmune Disease: Reading Inflammation in RA, Lupus, and Beyond
item.description: CRP tracks disease activity well in rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis, but is often normal or only mildly elevated in lupus. Understanding the CRP-ESR dissociation is key to reading autoimmune inflammation.

item.title: CRP and Exercise: How Workouts Affect Your Inflammation Reading
item.description: A single hard workout can transiently raise CRP for 1 to 3 days through muscle damage, while regular training lowers your baseline over time. Learn when to test around exercise.

item.title: The Paleo Diet and Inflammation: Does Eating Like an Ancestor Reduce CRP?
item.description: The paleo diet removes ultra-processed foods and refined sugar, which can lower CRP. But it also excludes legumes and whole grains that carry their own anti-inflammatory fiber. The evidence is mixed.

item.title: Prostatitis and Inflammation: Understanding the Inflamed Prostate
item.description: Prostatitis is one of the most common urological complaints in men, and inflammation sits at its center. Here is how the inflamed prostate causes pain.

item.title: Raynaud's and Inflammation: Blood Vessels, Autoimmunity, and Cold Hands
item.description: Raynaud's turns fingers white and blue in the cold. When it is secondary to autoimmune disease, inflammation of the blood vessels is often part of the story.

item.title: Red Light Therapy and Inflammation: What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: Red light therapy, or photobiomodulation, targets mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase to influence inflammation and recovery. The evidence for local inflammation is mixed but promising, and worth an honest look.

item.title: Shingles and Inflammation: The Inflammatory Nerve Attack of Reactivated Virus
item.description: Shingles occurs when the dormant varicella-zoster virus reactivates and inflames the nerves. Learn how neuroinflammation drives the rash and pain, and why it can linger as postherpetic neuralgia.

item.title: Vasculitis and Inflammation: When Blood Vessels Become Inflamed
item.description: Vasculitis is a group of diseases defined by inflammation of the blood vessels themselves. Learn how giant cell arteritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and others drive markedly elevated CRP and ESR.

item.title: The Carnivore Diet and Inflammation: Does an All-Meat Diet Help or Harm?
item.description: The carnivore diet has passionate advocates who report less inflammation. We separate the anecdotal elimination-diet benefits from the real concerns around fiber, polyphenols, and saturated fat.

item.title: CRP and Cancer: What Elevated Inflammation Does and Does Not Mean
item.description: Chronically elevated CRP is associated with higher risk and worse prognosis in some cancers, but CRP is nonspecific and cannot diagnose or screen for cancer. Here is what the science says.

item.title: CRP and Pregnancy: How Inflammation Changes and What Is Normal
item.description: CRP rises modestly during normal pregnancy and climbs further in labor. Learn how inflammation shifts across pregnancy, the associations with preeclampsia and infection, and why reference ranges need care.

item.title: Fatty Liver Disease and Inflammation: How NAFLD Becomes NASH
item.description: Fatty liver disease begins quietly, but inflammation is what turns simple fat accumulation into progressive liver damage. Here is how NAFLD becomes NASH.

item.title: Lyme Disease and Inflammation: The Immune Aftermath of Infection
item.description: Lyme disease triggers a powerful inflammatory response to the Borrelia bacterium. Learn how that inflammation causes symptoms and why it can persist as post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.

item.title: Osteoporosis and Inflammation: How Inflammatory Signals Weaken Bone
item.description: Bone is living tissue in constant renewal. Inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-alpha tip that balance toward breakdown, driving the bone loss of osteoporosis.

item.title: POTS and Inflammation: Autonomic Dysfunction and the Immune Connection
item.description: POTS causes a racing heart on standing, and a growing body of research links it to autoimmune and post-viral inflammation, autoantibodies, and overlap with Long COVID and MCAS.

item.title: Sjogren's Syndrome and Inflammation: When the Immune System Attacks Moisture Glands
item.description: Sjogren's syndrome is an autoimmune disease in which lymphocytes infiltrate the moisture-producing glands. Learn how chronic inflammation drives dry eyes, dry mouth, and systemic symptoms.

item.title: Tinnitus and Inflammation: Can Inflammation Cause Ringing in the Ears?
item.description: Emerging research links tinnitus to cochlear inflammation and neuroinflammation, with activated microglia in the auditory pathway. Here is what the evidence does and does not show.

item.title: The Vegan Diet and Inflammation: Does Going Plant-Based Lower CRP?
item.description: Whole-food vegan diets are rich in fiber and polyphenols that studies link to lower CRP. But ultra-processed vegan foods and nutrient gaps like B12 and omega-3 complicate the picture.

item.title: CRP After Surgery: The Normal Day-by-Day Pattern and When to Worry
item.description: CRP rises sharply after surgery, peaking around 2 to 3 days, then falls. Learn what the normal pattern looks like and why a secondary rise can signal infection.

item.title: Chronic Hives and Inflammation: What Drives Recurrent Urticaria
item.description: Chronic hives are driven by mast cells releasing histamine into the skin. Here is how that inflammatory process works and why it can persist for months or years.

item.title: Menopause and Inflammation: How Hormonal Change Raises Inflammatory Risk
item.description: The estrogen decline of menopause removes an anti-inflammatory brake, raising IL-6, TNF-alpha, CRP, and visceral fat. Here is how hormonal change reshapes inflammatory risk.

item.title: Ankylosing Spondylitis and Inflammation: Understanding Inflammatory Back Pain
item.description: Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory arthritis of the spine driven by HLA-B27 and the IL-23 and IL-17 axis. Here is what separates inflammatory back pain from ordinary back pain.

item.title: CRP and Cholesterol: Why Inflammation Matters as Much as LDL
item.description: Cholesterol and inflammation are two separate drivers of heart disease. Learn why CRP adds risk information beyond LDL and why both numbers matter for prevention.

item.title: Yoga and Inflammation: How a Mind-Body Practice Lowers CRP
item.description: Yoga does more than improve flexibility. Studies show it lowers IL-6, CRP, and cortisol through effects on the HPA axis and the vagus nerve. Here is how the science works.

item.title: hsCRP vs Standard CRP: What Is the Difference?
item.description: hsCRP and standard CRP measure the same protein but at different ranges. Learn why high-sensitivity CRP is used for cardiovascular risk and standard CRP for infection.

item.title: Psoriatic Arthritis and Inflammation: When Skin and Joints Both Flare
item.description: Psoriatic arthritis links inflamed skin and inflamed joints through a shared immune pathway. Here is how the IL-17 and IL-23 axis drives disease in both.

item.title: Vaping and Inflammation: What E-Cigarettes Do to Your Body
item.description: E-cigarettes are marketed as safer than smoking, but vaping drives oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and airway and systemic inflammation. Here is what the science shows.

item.title: CRP and Heart Attack Risk: What Your Inflammation Number Predicts
item.description: High-sensitivity CRP is an independent predictor of heart attack and stroke risk. Learn what the below 1, 1 to 3, and above 3 mg/L cutoffs mean for your heart.

item.title: Does Losing Weight Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: Yes. Losing weight, especially visceral fat, reliably lowers inflammatory markers like CRP and IL-6. Even a 5 to 10 percent weight loss produces measurable drops. Here is what the research shows and how much weight loss it takes.

item.title: Hashimoto's and Inflammation: The Autoimmune Attack on the Thyroid
item.description: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system inflames and gradually destroys the thyroid gland. Here is how that inflammation works.

item.title: The Ketogenic Diet and Inflammation: Does Keto Lower CRP?
item.description: Does the ketogenic diet lower inflammation? The evidence on keto and CRP is mixed, but the ketone BHB has genuine anti-inflammatory power. Here is what the science shows.

item.title: Leptin Resistance and Inflammation: The Hormone That Fights Weight Loss
item.description: Leptin is the hormone that tells your brain you are full. In leptin resistance, that signal stops getting through, so hunger stays high despite ample fat stores. Chronic inflammation is a key driver. Here is how the loop works and how to interrupt it.

item.title: Weight Loss Plateaus and Inflammation: Why the Scale Gets Stuck
item.description: A weight loss plateau is usually metabolic adaptation, water retention, and lost muscle, not a lack of willpower. Chronic inflammation can make plateaus worse by disrupting appetite and insulin signaling. Here is what is really happening and how to break through.

item.title: Hair Loss and Inflammation: The Inflammatory Roots of Shedding
item.description: Many kinds of hair loss share an inflammatory root. Learn how scalp inflammation, alopecia areata autoimmunity, and telogen effluvium drive shedding, and where CRP fits.

item.title: SIBO and Inflammation: How Bacterial Overgrowth Drives Gut Inflammation
item.description: SIBO is an overgrowth of bacteria in the small intestine that can drive gut inflammation, damage the barrier, and provoke immune activation. Here is how it works.

item.title: Anemia of Inflammation: How Chronic Inflammation Causes Low Iron
item.description: Anemia of inflammation is caused by chronic inflammation, not iron deficiency. Learn how hepcidin, IL-6, and ferritin explain why iron gets locked away from the body.

item.title: IBS and Inflammation: Is Irritable Bowel Syndrome Inflammatory?
item.description: IBS is not classically inflammatory, but research reveals low-grade immune activation, mast cells, and gut-brain signaling. Here is what inflammation means for IBS.

item.title: Atherosclerosis and Inflammation: Why Plaque Is an Inflammatory Disease
item.description: Atherosclerosis was long seen as passive cholesterol buildup. Modern science shows it is an inflammatory disease, from LDL oxidation to the CANTOS trial and CRP.

item.title: Pancreatitis and Inflammation: How the Pancreas Turns on Itself
item.description: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas driven by its own digestive enzymes. Learn how it develops, why CRP tracks severity, and what protects the pancreas.

item.title: Acute vs Chronic Inflammation
item.description: Acute inflammation is a fast, protective response to injury or infection that resolves in days. Chronic inflammation is prolonged, low-grade, and often silent, and it drives many long-term diseases. Here is how they differ and why it matters.

item.title: Can You Feel Inflammation?
item.description: Acute inflammation you can often feel: heat, redness, swelling, and pain are its classic signs. But chronic low-grade inflammation is frequently silent, producing only vague symptoms or none at all, which is exactly why a blood marker like CRP is useful. Here is the honest science.

item.title: Celiac Disease and Inflammation
item.description: Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten that causes inflammation and damage in the small intestine. The only effective treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, and it must be diagnosed before you remove gluten from your diet.

item.title: Does Berberine Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: Probably, to a moderate degree. Berberine has emerging evidence: meta-analyses of randomized trials, mostly in metabolic conditions, report reductions in CRP, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. But study quality is uneven. Here is the honest evidence.

item.title: Does Elderberry Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: Elderberry is rich in antioxidant anthocyanins and has real antiviral evidence, but direct human evidence that it lowers inflammation is limited and mixed. Some studies even show it can raise inflammatory cytokines. Here is an honest look at the science.

item.title: Does Fish Oil Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: Yes. Fish oil, rich in the omega-3s EPA and DHA, has some of the strongest evidence of any supplement for lowering inflammation. Meta-analyses show it significantly reduces CRP, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. Here is the evidence, dosing, and honest caveats.

item.title: Does Glucosamine Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: The evidence is weak and mixed. Glucosamine is mainly studied for osteoarthritis symptoms, with inconsistent results. Some cohort and small trial data hint at lower CRP, but this is far from proven. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Does Inflammation Cause Belly Fat?
item.description: The relationship between inflammation and belly fat is bidirectional. Visceral fat around the organs actively secretes inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and inflammation in turn worsens metabolic health. So it is less cause and effect than a two-way loop. Here is the science.

item.title: Does Inflammation Cause Brain Fog?
item.description: Inflammation is plausibly linked to brain fog. Cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-alpha can affect the brain, disrupt neurotransmitters, and impair cognition, and higher inflammatory markers are associated with cognitive decline. But 'brain fog' is a vague, multifactorial symptom. Here is the honest science.

item.title: Does Inflammation Cause Fatigue?
item.description: Inflammation is genuinely linked to fatigue. Cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-alpha drive the 'sickness behavior' that includes tiredness, and experimental studies confirm the connection. But fatigue has many causes, and inflammation is one contributor among several. Here is the science.

item.title: Does MSM Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: MSM (methylsulfonylmethane) has limited and mixed evidence for reducing inflammation. Small trials in knee osteoarthritis and exercise recovery suggest modest benefits, but meta-analyses often find effects that are not clinically meaningful. Here is the honest science.

item.title: Does NAC Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: The evidence is limited and mixed. NAC raises glutathione and has a plausible antioxidant mechanism, and some trials and a meta-analysis report lower CRP and IL-6. But results are inconsistent across doses and conditions. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Does Spirulina Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: Spirulina shows moderate, emerging evidence for lowering inflammation. Several randomized trials and meta-analyses report reductions in C-reactive protein, though effects on IL-6 and TNF-alpha are mixed. Here is an honest look at what the science supports.

item.title: Gallbladder Inflammation (Cholecystitis): Causes, CRP, and What Helps
item.description: Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, usually triggered by gallstones. Learn how it develops, why CRP rises sharply, and what helps calm the inflammation.

item.title: How to Reduce Inflammation in the Feet
item.description: Foot inflammation has many causes, from plantar fasciitis and tendinitis to gout, and each calls for a different approach. Here is how to distinguish localized foot problems from systemic inflammation, plus evidence-based measures like RICE, footwear, and weight.

item.title: How to Reduce Inflammation in the Neck
item.description: Neck inflammation is usually localized irritation from strain, poor posture, or wear, and it responds to rest, gentle movement, heat or ice, and better ergonomics. Here is how to tell localized neck issues from systemic inflammation and what actually helps.

item.title: Are Beans Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Beans and other legumes have a decent anti-inflammatory case, driven by fiber, resistant starch, and polyphenols. The popular fear that their lectins cause inflammation is largely a myth, since proper cooking neutralizes them. Here is the honest evidence.

item.title: Is Coconut Oil Inflammatory?
item.description: Coconut oil is not the anti-inflammatory superfood its marketing suggests. It is very high in saturated fat and raises LDL cholesterol, while meta-analyses find no significant effect on inflammation markers. The evidence for a benefit is weak. Here is the honest read.

item.title: Is Oat Milk Inflammatory? The Honest Answer
item.description: Oat milk is not meaningfully anti-inflammatory. It is a refined-carb beverage that is often low in fiber and can carry added oils and sugars, giving it a high glycemic response. Depending on the formulation it may be mildly unfavorable. Here is the honest breakdown.

item.title: Is Oatmeal Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Oatmeal is modestly anti-inflammatory, mainly because of its beta-glucan fiber. Meta-analyses of randomized trials link oats to lower CRP, with the clearest effect in people who are overweight or have existing conditions. Here is the honest evidence.

item.title: Is Peanut Butter Inflammatory?
item.description: Natural peanut butter, made from just peanuts, is roughly neutral to mildly favorable for inflammation, in line with the decent evidence for nuts. Commercial versions with added sugar and hydrogenated oils are a different story. Here is the nuance.

item.title: Is Quinoa Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Quinoa has a modest anti-inflammatory case. As a fiber-rich whole grain with polyphenols and complete protein, it fits an anti-inflammatory diet, but direct human trial evidence on quinoa itself is limited. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is Rice Inflammatory?
item.description: Rice is not strongly inflammatory, but it depends on the type. White rice is refined and high-glycemic, which can nudge inflammation up when eaten in excess, while brown rice keeps its fiber and antioxidants. Here is the honest, nuanced evidence.

item.title: Is Soda Inflammatory?
item.description: Yes, sugar-sweetened soda is genuinely pro-inflammatory, and the evidence is strong. A randomized trial found that even low to moderate intake raised markers of cardiovascular risk in weeks, and cohort studies link soda to higher CRP. Here is the evidence.

item.title: Are Sweet Potatoes Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Sweet potatoes have a modest anti-inflammatory case built on fiber, beta-carotene, and anthocyanin antioxidants. Much of the direct evidence is from cell and animal studies, so the human effect is real but modest. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is Wine Inflammatory?
item.description: On balance, wine is not anti-inflammatory. Ethanol itself is pro-inflammatory and heavy drinking clearly raises CRP. Any benefit from moderate red wine is small, contested, and easily undone. Here is the honest evidence.

item.title: Lupus and Inflammation
item.description: Lupus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, making inflammation central to the condition. It requires medical diagnosis and treatment. A notable quirk is that CRP is often disproportionately low during lupus flares.

item.title: Plantar Fasciitis and Inflammation
item.description: Despite its name, plantar fasciitis is now understood to be more of a degenerative condition (fasciosis) than a purely inflammatory one, similar to tendinosis. Here is what the tissue evidence shows, why it matters for treatment, and how to manage heel pain.

item.title: Sciatica and Inflammation
item.description: Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve caused by irritation or compression of a nerve root in the lower back, usually from a herniated disc. Inflammation around the nerve root contributes to the pain. Most cases are self-limiting and resolve within weeks.

item.title: Stroke and Inflammation: How Inflammation Raises Stroke Risk
item.description: Inflammation shapes stroke risk before an event and drives brain damage after one. Learn how CRP predicts risk and how post-stroke neuroinflammation affects recovery.

item.title: What Are the Best Anti-Inflammatory Breakfast Ideas?
item.description: The best anti-inflammatory breakfasts pair fiber-rich whole grains, berries, nuts, and unsweetened protein while skipping added sugar and refined carbs. Here is a week of simple ideas backed by evidence.

item.title: What Are the Best Anti-Inflammatory Herbs?
item.description: The best-evidenced anti-inflammatory herbs are turmeric, ginger, garlic, rosemary, cinnamon, and green tea. Here is what each active compound does and how strong the evidence is.

item.title: What Are the Best Anti-Inflammatory Snacks?
item.description: The best anti-inflammatory snacks are whole foods like nuts, berries, plain yogurt, and vegetables with hummus. Here are practical, evidence-based options to replace processed snacks.

item.title: What Are the Best Anti-Inflammatory Drinks? An Honest, Evidence-Ranked Guide
item.description: Water, green tea, tart cherry juice, coffee, and turmeric lattes are the drinks most often called anti-inflammatory. Here is an honest, evidence-ranked look at what each one actually does.

item.title: Are Chia Seeds Anti-Inflammatory? What the CRP Research Shows
item.description: Chia seeds are rich in ALA omega-3, fiber, and antioxidants. A meta-analysis found chia significantly lowered CRP, though the evidence base is small. Here is what the research supports, honestly.

item.title: Are Flax Seeds Anti-Inflammatory? What 54 Trials on CRP Show
item.description: Flax seeds have some of the better human evidence among anti-inflammatory foods. A meta-analysis of 54 randomized trials found flaxseed significantly lowered CRP and IL-6. Here is what the science supports.

item.title: Are Mushrooms Anti-Inflammatory? What Beta-Glucans and Ergothioneine Show
item.description: Mushrooms contain beta-glucans and ergothioneine, compounds with real anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity. The mechanisms are promising, but most human evidence is still early. Here is what the research supports.

item.title: Are Processed Meats Inflammatory? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Yes, processed meats are among the more genuinely inflammatory foods. The IARC classifies processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, and it combines nitrites, sodium, heme iron, and high-heat compounds linked to inflammation and disease. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Are Tomatoes Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Tomatoes have moderate anti-inflammatory evidence driven by lycopene. A trial of tomato juice lowered inflammatory markers in overweight women, though a study in healthy people showed no change in CRP. The benefit is real but depends on who you are.

item.title: How Are Bursitis and Inflammation Linked?
item.description: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa, a small fluid-filled sac that cushions joints. Learn the difference between non-infectious and septic bursitis, common causes, and when to see a doctor.

item.title: How Long Does Inflammation Last?
item.description: Acute inflammation lasts days to a few weeks; chronic inflammation lasts months to years. Learn the typical timelines, how CRP rises and falls, and when lingering inflammation warrants attention.

item.title: How Do You Reduce Inflammation in Your Body?
item.description: You reduce inflammation in the body through diet, regular exercise, quality sleep, weight management, not smoking, and stress reduction. Here is the evidence behind each lever and how to prioritize them.

item.title: How Do You Reduce Inflammation in Your Stomach?
item.description: Reducing stomach inflammation (gastritis) starts with treating the cause: H. pylori infection, NSAID use, or alcohol. Learn the common triggers, diet and lifestyle steps that help, and when to see a doctor.

item.title: Is Bacon Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: Yes, bacon carries a genuine inflammatory and disease signal. As a processed meat it combines nitrites, high sodium, saturated fat, and high-heat cooking compounds. The IARC classifies processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Broccoli Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Broccoli has a strong anti-inflammatory mechanism through sulforaphane, which activates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway. Human trial results are more mixed, with some short studies showing no marker change. Here is the honest evidence.

item.title: Is Butter Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: Butter has a mixed, modest relationship with inflammation. Some studies tie high saturated fat to higher CRP, but most controlled trials show little effect on inflammatory markers in healthy people. Amount and overall diet matter most. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Cheese Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: For most people cheese is not inflammatory. Controlled trials show cheese does not raise hs-CRP compared with low-fat diets, and as a fermented dairy food it is neutral to mildly favorable. The exceptions are milk allergy and intolerance. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Cinnamon Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Cinnamon has modest anti-inflammatory evidence. A meta-analysis of six trials found cinnamon supplements lowered CRP by about 0.81 mg/L, mostly in people with elevated baseline inflammation, and much of the benefit appears tied to blood sugar control.

item.title: Is Fast Food Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: Yes, fast food is genuinely pro-inflammatory. As ultra-processed food, it combines refined carbs, fried components, additives, and high sodium. A scoping review found most adult studies link higher ultra-processed intake to elevated CRP. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Fried Food Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: Yes, fried food is one of the more genuinely pro-inflammatory categories in the diet. High-heat frying creates advanced glycation end products, oxidized fats, and acrylamide that raise inflammatory markers like CRP and IL-6. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Ginger Tea Anti-Inflammatory? What the Gingerol Research Shows
item.description: Ginger tea carries the same anti-inflammatory gingerols as ginger, but in a lighter, more variable dose than the supplements used in trials. Here is what the research supports and where the limits are.

item.title: Is High-Fructose Corn Syrup Inflammatory?
item.description: High-fructose corn syrup is best seen as pro-inflammatory because it is a concentrated added sugar, not because it is chemically unique. Controlled trials show it behaves like table sugar gram for gram. Here is the honest evidence.

item.title: Is Kefir Anti-Inflammatory? What the Gut-Microbiome Research Shows
item.description: Kefir is a fermented milk drink rich in probiotics. A Stanford randomized trial found a fermented-food diet raised gut diversity and lowered inflammatory markers. Here is what the emerging evidence supports.

item.title: Is Kimchi Anti-Inflammatory? What the Fermented-Food Research Shows
item.description: Kimchi is a fermented vegetable dish rich in probiotics and plant compounds. A Stanford randomized trial found a fermented-food diet raised gut diversity and lowered inflammation. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is Margarine Inflammatory?
item.description: Old-style margarine made with partially hydrogenated oils was genuinely inflammatory because of trans fats. Modern trans-fat-free margarine is largely neutral in controlled trials. The answer depends entirely on which margarine you mean.

item.title: Is Matcha Anti-Inflammatory? What the EGCG Research Actually Shows
item.description: Matcha is concentrated green tea, rich in the catechin EGCG, which is anti-inflammatory in the lab. But randomized trials have not shown green tea reliably lowers CRP in humans. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is MSG Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: No, MSG is largely exonerated in controlled human studies. Monosodium glutamate is recognized as safe by the FDA, and human trials have not confirmed the reactions long blamed on it. The real caveats are sodium content and where MSG tends to appear. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Pineapple Anti-Inflammatory? What the Research on Bromelain Shows
item.description: Pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme with genuine anti-inflammatory activity, especially in post-surgical swelling. But most evidence uses concentrated bromelain, not the fruit. Here is what the science supports.

item.title: Is Pork Inflammatory?
item.description: Processed pork such as bacon, sausage, and ham is linked to higher inflammatory markers, while lean fresh pork appears modest to neutral once body weight is accounted for. The processing, not the pig, drives most of the signal.

item.title: Is Salmon Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Yes, salmon is one of the best-supported anti-inflammatory foods, thanks to its high content of the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA. An umbrella meta-analysis found omega-3s significantly lower CRP, TNF-alpha, and IL-6. Here is the evidence.

item.title: Is Salt Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: Salt has an emerging but not simple link to inflammation. A landmark 2013 Nature study found high salt drives pro-inflammatory Th17 immune cells, and it clearly raises blood pressure, but the human inflammation picture is still developing. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Sauerkraut Anti-Inflammatory? What the Fermented-Food Research Shows
item.description: Sauerkraut is fermented cabbage rich in live probiotics, fiber, and vitamin C. A Stanford randomized trial found a fermented-food diet raised gut diversity and lowered inflammation. Here is the honest read.

item.title: Is Shellfish Inflammatory?
item.description: For most people shellfish is not inflammatory and may be mildly anti-inflammatory thanks to its omega-3 content and low saturated fat. The real caveats are shellfish allergy and how it is prepared, not the food itself.

item.title: Is Spinach Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Spinach is a modestly anti-inflammatory leafy green, rich in dietary nitrates that support blood vessel health plus lutein, folate, vitamin K, and magnesium. Most evidence comes from vegetable-rich diet patterns rather than spinach alone. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is Turmeric Anti-Inflammatory?
item.description: Yes, turmeric has real anti-inflammatory evidence through its compound curcumin. A meta-analysis of 32 trials found curcumin lowered CRP by about 1.55 mg/L. The catch is bioavailability: culinary turmeric is poorly absorbed. Here is the honest picture.

item.title: Is White Bread Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: White bread can modestly raise inflammation, mainly through its high glycemic load rather than the bread itself. Studies link high-glycemic-index diets to higher CRP, and low-GI diets lower hs-CRP. Whole grains behave better. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Is Yogurt Inflammatory? What the Evidence Actually Shows
item.description: No, yogurt is not inflammatory. Plain yogurt is one of the more anti-inflammatory foods in the dairy aisle. A meta-analysis found probiotic yogurt lowered CRP, especially in overweight people. The catch is added sugar in flavored yogurt. Here is the full picture.

item.title: How Are Sinusitis and Inflammation Linked?
item.description: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinus lining. Acute sinusitis lasts under 4 weeks and is usually viral; chronic sinusitis lasts 12 weeks or more and involves ongoing inflammation. Learn the difference and when to see a doctor.

item.title: How Are Tendinitis and Inflammation Linked?
item.description: Tendinitis means inflammation of a tendon, but research shows many chronic tendon problems are more degeneration than inflammation. Learn the difference, how tendinitis develops, and when to see a doctor.

item.title: What Causes Inflammation in the Body?
item.description: Inflammation is caused by the immune system responding to threats like infection, injury, toxins, and stressors. Learn the difference between helpful acute inflammation and harmful chronic inflammation, and what triggers each.

item.title: What Is a Normal CRP Level? Chart by Age and Full Ranges
item.description: A normal hs-CRP level is below 1.0 mg/L. Learn the full CRP reference range chart, how levels shift with age, and the difference between standard CRP and hs-CRP.

item.title: Is Rosacea an Inflammatory Skin Condition?
item.description: Rosacea is an inflammatory skin disorder rooted in an overactive innate immune system. Excess cathelicidin (LL-37) drives the redness and visible vessels. Here is how the inflammation works.

item.title: What Are the Signs of Chronic Inflammation?
item.description: Common signs of chronic inflammation include persistent fatigue, joint pain and stiffness, digestive issues, brain fog, and slow recovery. Learn the symptoms and how CRP helps make them measurable.

item.title: Can You Test Inflammation at Home? What Actually Works
item.description: Yes, you can test inflammation at home by measuring CRP from a finger-prick sample. Learn how at-home CRP testing works, how accurate it is, and what it can and cannot tell you.

item.title: Is Coffee Inflammatory? What the Research Shows
item.description: For most people coffee is not inflammatory and is net anti-inflammatory. Reviews of randomized trials find coffee lowers markers of oxidative stress and inflammation, especially with regular long-term intake. Added sugar and cream are the real concern. Here is the evidence.

item.title: Is Chocolate Inflammatory? Dark vs Milk Chocolate
item.description: Dark chocolate and cocoa are net anti-inflammatory for most people. A meta-analysis found cocoa products lowered C-reactive protein by about 0.98 mg/L over the long term. Milk chocolate and candy are different because of high sugar. Here is the cocoa-vs-candy breakdown.

item.title: Is Bone Broth Anti-Inflammatory? What the Thin Evidence Shows
item.description: Bone broth is popular for inflammation, but the human evidence is thin. Its collagen, glycine, and minerals are plausible but largely unproven, and there are no strong human trials on bone broth and inflammation.

item.title: Is Avocado Anti-Inflammatory? Monounsaturated Fat and Fiber
item.description: Avocado supports an anti-inflammatory diet through monounsaturated fat, fiber, and carotenoids. A 12-week randomized trial found daily avocado significantly lowered C-reactive protein in adults with insulin resistance.

item.title: How Do You Reduce Inflammation in Your Back?
item.description: You reduce back inflammation by staying active rather than resting in bed, strengthening the core and back, improving posture, managing weight, and eating an anti-inflammatory diet. A practical guide.

item.title: How Do You Reduce Inflammation in Your Knees?
item.description: You reduce knee inflammation by strengthening supporting muscles, keeping a healthy weight, using low-impact movement and RICE for flare-ups, and eating an anti-inflammatory diet. A practical guide.

item.title: How Do You Reduce Inflammation in Your Joints?
item.description: You reduce joint inflammation with regular low-impact movement, a healthy weight, an anti-inflammatory diet, quality sleep, and stress management. Here is an evidence-based, practical guide.

item.title: How Do You Reduce Inflammation Quickly? What Works and What Doesn't
item.description: You can reduce acute inflammation quickly with rest, sleep, hydration, and anti-inflammatory foods, but chronic inflammation takes weeks to lower. Learn what actually works fast and what is oversold.

item.title: How Do You Lower CRP Levels? Evidence-Based Ways to Reduce Inflammation
item.description: You lower CRP by targeting what drives it: losing visceral fat, exercising regularly, eating an anti-inflammatory diet, quitting smoking, sleeping well, and managing stress. Here is the evidence.

item.title: How Often Should You Test Your CRP?
item.description: For a reliable baseline, take two CRP readings about two weeks apart and average them. For tracking lifestyle changes, monthly or every few weeks works well. Learn the ideal CRP testing cadence.

item.title: What Does a High CRP Level Mean? Causes and What to Do
item.description: A high CRP means active inflammation. An hs-CRP above 3.0 mg/L signals elevated low-grade inflammation, while above 10 mg/L usually points to acute infection or injury. Learn the causes.

item.title: How Are Gout and Inflammation Linked?
item.description: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis. Monosodium urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing IL-1 beta and driving the sudden pain of a gout flare. Here is how it works.

item.title: Is GERD Caused by Inflammation, Not Just Acid?
item.description: GERD may be as much an inflammatory condition as a chemical one. A JAMA study found reflux esophagitis develops through a cytokine-mediated immune response, not just acid burning the esophagus.

item.title: Do You Need to Fast Before a CRP Test? No, Here Is Why
item.description: No, a CRP or hs-CRP test does not require fasting on its own. You only need to fast if the CRP is bundled with a test that does, such as a lipid panel or fasting glucose. Here is how to prepare.

item.title: Does Zinc Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Zinc shows mixed but promising evidence for inflammation. A meta-analysis of 73 studies found zinc lowered CRP by about 0.75 mg/L in adults but not in children. Here is the real evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Does Vitamin C Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Vitamin C shows inconsistent evidence for inflammation overall, but several randomized trials find it lowers CRP in people who are older, deficient, or already have high CRP. Here is the real evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Does Tart Cherry Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Tart cherry has solid evidence for reducing exercise-related inflammation and speeding recovery. A meta-analysis of 14 studies found it lowered CRP and interleukin-6 and improved muscle recovery. Here is the real evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Does Quercetin Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Quercetin has strong laboratory anti-inflammatory activity but modest human evidence. A meta-analysis found no overall effect on CRP, with a small reduction only in people who already had a diagnosed disease. Here is the honest evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Does Magnesium Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Magnesium shows moderate evidence for reducing inflammation. Meta-analyses find it lowers CRP most clearly in people whose CRP is already above 3 mg/L. Here is the real evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Does Collagen Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Collagen has real evidence for joint pain and function but is not primarily an inflammation-marker story. Randomized trials show reduced osteoarthritis pain, while direct CRP-lowering data is limited. Here is the honest evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Can Inflammation Cause Weight Gain? What the Scale Won't Tell You
item.description: Chronic inflammation drives belly fat, insulin resistance, and leptin resistance. Learn why the scale misleads and how tracking inflammation can support your weight goals.

item.title: Go Beyond the Scale: 5 Wellness Markers That Matter More Than Weight
item.description: Weight is just one number. Discover 5 wellness markers that give a fuller picture of your health, including inflammation, sleep, and body composition.

item.title: Does CBD Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: CBD has strong anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory and animal studies, but human trials measuring inflammation markers are thin, and there are real regulatory caveats. Here is the honest evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: GLP-1 Medications and Inflammation: What You Should Know
item.description: GLP-1 medications like Ozempic may reduce inflammation alongside weight loss. Learn how CRP tracking helps you understand your body's response to any treatment.

item.title: Does Boswellia Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Boswellia serrata has reasonable randomized-trial evidence for reducing joint inflammation and pain in osteoarthritis, with benefits reported in as little as 7 days at 100 mg per day. Here is the real evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Does Ashwagandha Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Ashwagandha has limited direct evidence for lowering inflammation markers, and its strongest data is for stress and cortisol. A meta-analysis of 9 trials found it lowered cortisol and perceived stress. Here is the honest evidence, dose, and safety.

item.title: Do Probiotics Reduce Inflammation? What the Evidence Shows
item.description: Probiotics show strain-specific and population-specific evidence for inflammation. Meta-analyses find they can lower CRP in people with chronic conditions, but the effect depends on the strain and who is taking it. Here is the real evidence.

item.title: CRP vs ESR: Which Inflammation Marker Matters?
item.description: CRP and ESR both measure inflammation, but CRP responds within hours and reflects current inflammation, while ESR changes over days. Compare the two markers and when each is used.

item.title: How Much Does a CRP Test Cost in 2026? Full Price Breakdown
item.description: A CRP test costs roughly $8 to $50 at direct-to-consumer labs and can reach $75 to $250 at hospitals without insurance. hs-CRP tends to cost slightly more. Here is a full price breakdown.

item.title: What If Your CRP Is Normal but You Still Feel Inflamed?
item.description: A normal CRP does not rule out inflammation. CRP is a nonspecific, whole-body marker that can miss localized, chronic, or low-grade inflammation. Here is why, and what to do next.

item.title: What Does CRP Tell You About Long COVID?
item.description: CRP can be elevated in some people with long COVID but is often normal, so it cannot confirm or rule out the condition. Learn what inflammation markers show in long COVID research and how to read a result.

item.title: Normal CRP Levels in Children: A Parent's Guide by Age
item.description: A normal CRP in older children is generally below 3 mg/L, while newborns can normally read up to about 10 mg/L in the first days of life. Learn pediatric CRP reference ranges and why a doctor must interpret them.

item.title: How Is Asthma Linked to Inflammation?
item.description: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways. In most people it is driven by type 2 inflammation involving IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and eosinophils. Here is how airway inflammation works.

item.title: Are Seed Oils Inflammatory? What the Human Evidence Shows
item.description: Despite the popular claim, human trials do not show that seed oils cause inflammation. A meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials found increasing linoleic acid did not raise C-reactive protein. Harvard experts call the pro-inflammatory theory unsupported. Here is the evidence.

item.title: Are Nuts Anti-Inflammatory? Omega-3 ALA, Fiber, and Polyphenols
item.description: Nuts support an anti-inflammatory diet through ALA omega-3 fats, fiber, vitamin E, and polyphenols. A meta-analysis of 32 trials found nuts improved blood vessel function, though their direct effect on CRP was small.

item.title: Are Nightshades Inflammatory? What the Evidence Says
item.description: There is no strong human evidence that nightshade vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant cause inflammation. The Arthritis Foundation calls it a myth, and many nightshades are rich in anti-inflammatory antioxidants. Here is the full picture.

item.title: Are Leafy Greens Anti-Inflammatory? Nitrates, Folate, and Vitamin K
item.description: Yes, leafy greens like spinach and kale are anti-inflammatory. They deliver dietary nitrate, folate, vitamin K, magnesium, and carotenoids, and higher intake is consistently linked to lower inflammation markers.

item.title: Are Eggs Inflammatory? What the Research Shows
item.description: For most people eggs are not inflammatory. A 2022 review found eggs have neutral effects on inflammatory biomarkers, and several trials show no rise in C-reactive protein. Eggs also contain anti-inflammatory nutrients. Here is the evidence.

item.title: Are Berries Anti-Inflammatory? The Anthocyanin Evidence
item.description: Yes, berries are anti-inflammatory. Their anthocyanins give them their color and modest CRP-lowering effects. A meta-analysis of 44 trials found anthocyanin-rich berries significantly reduced C-reactive protein.

item.title: Are Artificial Sweeteners Inflammatory? The Mixed Evidence
item.description: The evidence on artificial sweeteners and inflammation is genuinely mixed. Some show gut-microbiome changes and cohort links to cardiovascular risk, while long-term studies show no clear inflammatory effect. Here is an honest look at what is known and unknown.

item.title: A 7-Day Anti-Inflammatory Meal Plan
item.description: A practical anti-inflammatory meal plan built on the Mediterranean pattern, with a 7-day framework, food swaps, and foods to limit. Grounded in research linking this diet to lower CRP and IL-6.

item.title: Inflammation and Longevity: What the Science of Long Life Reveals
item.description: The science of longevity increasingly points to inflammation control as a central mechanism. Learn what blue zone populations, centenarian studies, and longevity research reveal about keeping inflammation low for a longer, healthier life.

item.title: Understanding Your CRP: What the Numbers Actually Mean
item.description: CRP is the most widely used marker of systemic inflammation. Learn what different CRP levels mean, what can cause them to rise, and how to interpret trends over time.

item.title: Hydration and Inflammation: The Overlooked Connection
item.description: Chronic mild dehydration elevates inflammatory markers and impairs the body's ability to clear inflammatory waste. Learn how hydration status affects CRP and systemic inflammation.

item.title: Exercise, Recovery, and Inflammation: How to Train Smarter
item.description: Exercise triggers a brief inflammatory response that drives adaptation. But too much training without adequate recovery can tip into chronic inflammation. Learn how to balance the two.

item.title: Fibromyalgia and Inflammation: Rethinking Widespread Pain
item.description: Fibromyalgia has long been considered a non-inflammatory condition. New research on neuroinflammation and central sensitization is fundamentally changing that view.

item.title: ME/CFS and Inflammation: When the Immune System Fails to Reset
item.description: Myalgic encephalomyelitis and chronic fatigue syndrome involve persistent neuroinflammation and immune dysregulation. Learn what the latest research reveals about the inflammatory biology of ME/CFS.

item.title: Noise Pollution and Inflammation: The Overlooked Environmental Health Risk
item.description: Chronic noise exposure activates the stress axis and disrupts sleep in ways that chronically elevate CRP and cardiovascular inflammatory markers. Here is what the evidence shows about traffic noise, health outcomes, and protection.

item.title: Microplastics and Inflammation: An Emerging Environmental Threat to Immune Health
item.description: Microplastics and nanoplastics have been detected in human blood, lungs, liver, placenta, and arterial plaques. Here is what the evidence shows about their inflammatory effects and what you can do to reduce exposure.

item.title: How Inflammation Ages Your Skin: The Science of Inflammaging from the Outside In
item.description: Skin aging is more than sun damage and genetics. Chronic systemic inflammation accelerates every visible sign of aging from within. Here is what the research shows.

item.title: Can Weather Affect Your Inflammation? What the Research Shows
item.description: Cold temperatures, dropping barometric pressure, seasonal vitamin D loss, and air pollution all measurably affect inflammation levels. Here is what the science shows.

item.title: Mitochondria and Inflammation: How Your Cellular Power Plants Control Immune Response
item.description: Damaged mitochondria release pro-inflammatory signals that activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and cGAS-STING pathway. Mitochondrial health is inseparable from inflammatory health.

item.title: Estrogen and Inflammation: Why Menopause Changes Your Inflammatory Profile
item.description: Estrogen suppresses NF-kB activity and promotes anti-inflammatory immune regulation. The menopausal drop in estrogen removes this protection, explaining the sharp rise in cardiovascular and inflammatory disease risk after menopause.

item.title: Testosterone and Inflammation: The Hormonal Link Between Low T and Chronic Disease
item.description: Testosterone has direct anti-inflammatory effects on immune cells and vasculature. Low testosterone is consistently associated with elevated CRP and IL-6, and the relationship is bidirectional.

item.title: Fertility and Inflammation: How Chronic Immune Activation Affects Reproductive Health
item.description: Chronic inflammation impairs ovarian reserve, disrupts implantation, reduces sperm quality, and increases miscarriage risk through well-characterized immunological mechanisms.

item.title: Endometriosis and Inflammation: Why Immune Dysfunction Is Central to This Condition
item.description: Endometriosis is fundamentally a disease of immune dysregulation in which the peritoneal environment fails to clear ectopic endometrial tissue. Chronic peritoneal inflammation drives lesion growth and systemic symptoms.

item.title: PCOS and Inflammation: The Hormonal Disorder with an Inflammatory Root
item.description: Polycystic ovary syndrome involves insulin resistance, androgen excess, and chronic low-grade inflammation that reinforce each other. Here is the biology and what anti-inflammatory strategies show in clinical research.

item.title: The Mediterranean Diet and Inflammation: The Best-Studied Anti-Inflammatory Eating Pattern
item.description: The Mediterranean diet reduces CRP by up to 41 percent in randomized trials. Here is what makes it work, what the PREDIMED trial showed, and how to adopt it practically.

item.title: Ultra-Processed Foods and Inflammation: Why the Modern Diet Is an Inflammatory One
item.description: Ultra-processed foods contain emulsifiers, preservatives, and additives that disrupt the gut barrier and microbiome, raising CRP and driving chronic disease independently of their poor nutritional profile.

item.title: Is Acne Caused by Inflammation?
item.description: Acne is a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicle and oil gland. Cutibacterium acnes activates the innate immune system, releasing IL-1, IL-8, and TNF. Here is how the inflammation works.

item.title: Why Does Sugar Cause Inflammation?
item.description: Excess dietary sugar elevates CRP through multiple distinct pathways: postprandial NF-kB activation, fructose-driven liver inflammation, and advanced glycation end product accumulation. Here is the complete picture.

item.title: Hypertension and Inflammation: The Vascular Link Between Pressure and Immune Activation
item.description: High blood pressure and chronic inflammation reinforce each other through endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and renin-angiotensin system activation. Here is the bidirectional biology.

item.title: Metabolic Syndrome and Inflammation: The Five-Factor Cluster Behind Chronic Disease
item.description: Metabolic syndrome links abdominal obesity, high blood sugar, high triglycerides, low HDL, and high blood pressure through a shared inflammatory mechanism. Here is the biology connecting them.

item.title: IBD and Inflammation: The Science Behind Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis
item.description: Inflammatory bowel disease involves dysregulated mucosal immune responses in the gut with systemic consequences. Here is the immunological biology, the gut microbiome role, and what drives flares and remission.

item.title: Alzheimer's Disease and Neuroinflammation: New Evidence for an Old Enemy
item.description: The amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease is being revised to incorporate neuroinflammation as a central driver, not just a bystander. Here is what the latest evidence shows about microglia, APOE4, and lifestyle prevention.

item.title: Parkinson's Disease and Neuroinflammation: The Gut-Brain Axis Connection
item.description: Neuroinflammation and microglial activation are central to Parkinson's disease progression. Emerging evidence suggests the disease may begin in the gut years before motor symptoms appear.

item.title: Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroinflammation: What Goes Wrong in the Immune System
item.description: Multiple sclerosis is driven by T-cell-mediated neuroinflammation that destroys the myelin sheath. Here is the immunological biology behind the disease and what emerging research shows about modifiable inflammatory factors.

item.title: Eczema and Inflammation: The Immune Imbalance Behind Atopic Dermatitis
item.description: Atopic dermatitis is driven by Th2 immune skewing and skin barrier dysfunction that creates a cycle of inflammation, itching, and barrier damage. Here is what the research shows about its systemic connections.

item.title: Psoriasis and Systemic Inflammation: More Than a Skin Condition
item.description: Psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory disease that raises cardiovascular risk, worsens metabolic health, and drives joint destruction. Here is the biology behind why skin disease has whole-body consequences.

item.title: Thyroid Disease and Inflammation: The Autoimmune Connection Most People Miss
item.description: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism, and it is fundamentally an inflammatory autoimmune disease. Understanding the inflammation-thyroid connection changes how the condition should be managed.

item.title: Anxiety and Inflammation: The Bidirectional Relationship Linking Mental and Physical Health
item.description: Anxiety disorders are associated with elevated CRP and IL-6. Anti-inflammatory interventions reduce anxiety symptoms in clinical trials. Here is the biology connecting fear pathways and immune activation.

item.title: Sarcopenia and Inflammation: Why You Lose Muscle as You Age
item.description: Chronic inflammation is one of the primary drivers of age-related muscle loss. Learn what sarcopenia is, how inflammation accelerates it, and what you can do about it.

item.title: Sitting Is the New Smoking: How a Sedentary Lifestyle Fuels Chronic Inflammation
item.description: Prolonged sitting activates inflammatory pathways independently of total exercise volume. Even people who meet weekly exercise guidelines show elevated CRP if they sit for most of the day.

item.title: Sauna and Inflammation: Why Heat Therapy Rivals Exercise as an Anti-Inflammatory Tool
item.description: Regular sauna use reduces CRP, IL-6, and cardiovascular mortality with effect sizes comparable to moderate aerobic exercise. Here is the biology behind the Finnish research and what protocols work best.

item.title: Cold Exposure and Inflammation: The Science Behind Cold Plunges and Ice Baths
item.description: Cold water immersion activates norepinephrine release and hormetic stress responses that reduce systemic inflammation. Here is what the clinical evidence shows about protocols, benefits, and who benefits most.

item.title: Autophagy and Inflammation: How Cellular Self-Cleaning Prevents Chronic Disease
item.description: Autophagy removes the damaged proteins, dysfunctional mitochondria, and cellular debris that trigger inflammasome activation and chronic inflammation. Here is how to support it.

item.title: Dietary Fiber and Inflammation: Why Your Gut Bacteria Need You to Eat More Plants
item.description: Dietary fiber feeds gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, which strengthen the gut barrier and directly suppress NF-kB signaling. High-fiber diets consistently reduce CRP in clinical trials.

item.title: Resveratrol and Inflammation: The Red Wine Compound Under the Microscope
item.description: Resveratrol activates SIRT1 and inhibits NF-kB in animal models with impressive results. Human trials have been more mixed. Here is what the evidence actually shows.

item.title: Curcumin and Inflammation: Does Turmeric Actually Work?
item.description: Curcumin inhibits NF-kB and reduces CRP in clinical trials. But the bioavailability problem is real. Here is what the evidence shows about which forms work, what doses matter, and who benefits most.

item.title: The Top Inflammatory Foods: What to Reduce and Why
item.description: Trans fats, refined carbohydrates, ultra-processed foods, and certain cooking methods each activate inflammatory pathways through distinct mechanisms. Here is the evidence behind the most reliably pro-inflammatory dietary patterns.

item.title: Inflammation and Bone Loss: The Hidden Driver of Osteoporosis
item.description: Chronic inflammation disrupts the balance between bone formation and bone breakdown, quietly driving osteoporosis. Here's what the research shows and what you can do about it.

item.title: Circadian Rhythm and Inflammation: Why Your Body Clock Controls Your Immune System
item.description: The circadian clock directly regulates inflammatory gene expression. Disrupting your body clock through shift work, late eating, or irregular sleep elevates CRP and raises chronic disease risk.

item.title: Red Meat and Inflammation: Separating the Science from the Headlines
item.description: The relationship between red meat and inflammation is more nuanced than most headlines suggest. Here is what the evidence actually shows about saturated fat, processed meat, TMAO, and inflammatory markers.

item.title: The Biology of Loneliness: How Social Isolation Triggers Chronic Inflammation
item.description: Loneliness activates a specific inflammatory gene expression pattern that evolved as a survival response. In modern life, chronic social isolation sustains this pattern in ways that directly damage health.

item.title: Long COVID and Inflammation: What Persistent Immune Activation Tells Us
item.description: Long COVID affects tens of millions of people globally. The emerging evidence points to persistent viral reservoirs, autoimmune activation, and chronic neuroinflammation as the primary drivers of prolonged symptoms.

item.title: Chronic Pain and Inflammation: The Cycle That Keeps You Stuck
item.description: Chronic pain and inflammation reinforce each other through central sensitization and neuroinflammatory mechanisms. Here is what the research shows about breaking this cycle.

item.title: Sleep Apnea and Chronic Inflammation: Why Disrupted Breathing Inflames Your Body
item.description: Obstructive sleep apnea causes repeated episodes of low oxygen that activate systemic inflammatory pathways. Here is how intermittent hypoxia drives CRP elevation and cardiovascular risk beyond what poor sleep alone explains.

item.title: Polyphenols and Inflammation: The Plant Compounds with Real Anti-Inflammatory Evidence
item.description: Polyphenols from berries, olive oil, green tea, and dark chocolate have well-documented anti-inflammatory effects. Here is what the research shows about which compounds work best and why bioavailability matters.

item.title: Vitamin D and Inflammation: The Deficiency Most People Do Not Know They Have
item.description: Vitamin D functions as an immune-regulating hormone. Deficiency is widespread and consistently associated with elevated inflammatory markers. Here is what the research shows about supplementation and inflammation.

item.title: Meditation, Mindfulness, and Inflammation: The Mind-Body Science
item.description: Mindfulness-based interventions reduce CRP and pro-inflammatory cytokines in multiple clinical trials. Here is the neuroimmunology behind how mental practice changes immune function.

item.title: Intermittent Fasting and Inflammation: What the Research Actually Shows
item.description: Intermittent fasting reduces inflammatory markers in multiple clinical trials. Here is what happens metabolically during the fasted state, and how time-restricted eating differs from extended fasting.

item.title: Air Pollution and Inflammation: The Invisible Threat to Your Immune System
item.description: Particulate matter and toxic gases from air pollution activate inflammatory pathways in the lungs and bloodstream. Here is what the research shows about the invisible link between the air you breathe and chronic disease.

item.title: Gum Disease and Systemic Inflammation: The Mouth-Body Connection
item.description: Periodontitis is the most common chronic infectious disease in humans and one of the most underappreciated drivers of systemic inflammation. The bacteria in your gums affect your heart, blood sugar, and brain.

item.title: Kidney Disease and Chronic Inflammation: A Dangerous Feedback Loop
item.description: The kidneys both regulate and are damaged by inflammatory processes. In chronic kidney disease, this relationship becomes a vicious cycle that accelerates organ decline and systemic disease.

item.title: Liver Inflammation and Metabolic Disease: The Silent Epidemic of NAFLD
item.description: The liver is the body's primary filter for inflammatory signals. When it becomes chronically inflamed, the effects ripple through every organ system. Here is what you need to know about NAFLD and hepatic inflammation.

item.title: Autoimmune Disease and Inflammation: When the Immune System Turns on Itself
item.description: In autoimmune conditions, inflammation is not a response to a pathogen. It is a misdirected attack on the body's own tissues. Understanding what drives this immune dysregulation is central to managing it.

item.title: How Does Inflammation Affect Your Brain?
item.description: Chronic systemic inflammation breaches the blood-brain barrier and activates microglia, contributing to cognitive decline, Alzheimer's, and brain fog.

item.title: How Are Obesity and Inflammation Linked?
item.description: Excess adipose tissue is an active endocrine organ that continuously secretes inflammatory signals. This is why obesity and chronic disease are so closely linked.

item.title: How Does Smoking Cause Inflammation?
item.description: Smoking is one of the most potent drivers of systemic chronic inflammation known to medicine. Here is the molecular biology behind why, and what happens to inflammation after quitting.

item.title: Alcohol and Inflammation: The Science Behind the Immune Disruption
item.description: Alcohol's effects on inflammation are complex, dose-dependent, and frequently misrepresented. Here is what the research actually shows about drinking and your immune system.

item.title: Do Omega-3s Reduce Inflammation?
item.description: Omega-3 fatty acids have one of the strongest evidence bases of any dietary intervention for reducing systemic inflammation. Here is what the clinical research shows.

item.title: Why Is Exercise the Best Anti-Inflammatory Medicine?
item.description: Exercise temporarily raises inflammatory markers, yet regular exercisers have the lowest chronic inflammation. Understanding this paradox is key to using movement as medicine.

item.title: How Does Stress Cause Inflammation?
item.description: Chronic psychological stress raises CRP, IL-6, and TNF-alpha in ways that parallel infection. Learn the biology behind stress-driven inflammation and how to interrupt it.

item.title: The Inflammation-Depression Connection: Is Your Immune System Affecting Your Mood?
item.description: Emerging research reveals that chronic inflammation may drive depression through cytokine signaling, microglial activation, and neuroinflammation pathways.

item.title: COPD and Inflammation: Understanding the Lung-Immune Connection
item.description: How COPD drives inflammation, from inflammatory cells to systemic inflammation and markers like CRP and fibrinogen, and what marker trends mean for wellness.

item.title: Inflammation: The Common Thread Behind Nearly Every Chronic Disease
item.description: Chronic inflammation is linked to heart disease, diabetes, cancer, and more. Learn why it is the root cause of most chronic diseases and how to monitor it.

item.title: The Inflammation-Cancer Connection: What Research Reveals
item.description: Explore the research linking chronic inflammation to cancer development and progression. Learn why tracking your inflammation markers matters for long-term health.

item.title: Silent Inflammation: The Hidden Driver Behind Chronic Disease
item.description: Silent inflammation has no obvious symptoms but fuels chronic disease over time. Learn how to detect it early with at-home CRP testing from Sensa Wellness.

item.title: Arthritis and Inflammation: Why Your Joints Are Telling You Something Important
item.description: Discover the role inflammation plays in arthritis and joint pain. Learn how tracking CRP levels at home with Sensa can fit into a healthy lifestyle.

item.title: The Anti-Inflammatory Diet: What the Science Actually Says
item.description: From the PREDIMED trial to omega-3 eicosanoids and gut microbiome science, here is what the evidence actually supports about anti-inflammatory eating.

item.title: Allergies and Inflammation: Your Immune System's Overreaction
item.description: Allergies trigger an inflammatory immune response that can affect your whole body. Learn how Sensa helps you track inflammation levels during allergy season.
